blocks.title: Biodegradable plastic
blocks.text: A biodegradable plastic is naturally decomposed by microorganisms into simpler, non-toxic compounds when buried for a certain period.

Plastics that contain natural polymers, such as starch, are degraded faster, because soil bacteria attack natural polymers easily. Polyesters and polyamides are more biodegradable than poly(alkene)s, because soil organisms, and also acids and alkalis, can hydrolyse their ester and amide links into simpler parts: polyamides give carboxylic acids and amines, and polyesters give carboxylic acids and alcohols. For example, poly(lactic acid) (PLA) can increase the biodegradability of a plastic. Some medical implants and dissolvable stitches are made from polyesters that slowly break down in the body by hydrolysis.

blocks.alt: Three panels. Poly(alkene)s: -CH2-CH2-CH2-, only strong non-polar bonds, chemically inert, persist (landfill, litter, harm to animals, microplastics). Biodegradable: -CO-O- and -CO-NH- links hydrolysed by acids, alkalis and soil microorganisms, giving acids and alcohols or acids and amines (e.g. PLA). Photodegradable: -CH2-CO-CH2- whose C=O absorbs UV light, weakening bonds; but short life, poor recycling and no light in landfill.
blocks.caption: Why some polymers degrade and others do not (original diagram for topics 26.5 to 26.5.2).
blocks.long_description: Whether a polymer degrades depends on the bonds in its chain. Chains of only C-C and C-H bonds have nothing for water or microbes to attack. Ester and amide links can be hydrolysed. Carbonyl groups absorb ultraviolet light, which breaks bonds and helps the plastic fall apart.

blocks.prompt: Why is a polyester more biodegradable than poly(ethene)?
blocks.explanation: Its ester links can be hydrolysed (by acids, alkalis or soil organisms) into carboxylic acids and alcohols, whereas poly(ethene) has only inert C-C and C-H bonds.

items: Polyesters and polyamides hydrolyse at ester and amide links (PLA, dissolvable stitches).
